sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Panoramic cameras capture nearly the entire spherical field of view in a single frame. However, the mismatch between this panoramic coverage and the field of view of LiDAR poses a substantial challenge for panoramic Gaussian splatting SLAM that relies on LiDAR depth priors. We introduce GOLD-SLAM, a Gaussian-splatting Omnidirectional LiDAR-Depth SLAM system that combines high-quality rendering with accurate geometric reconstruction. It performs tracking and mapping in the spherical domain and uses tracked visual features in regions without LiDAR coverage to improve pose estimation. To address insufficient coverage of newly observed surfaces and floating artifacts during incremental mapping, we introduce Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP). To enable broader evaluation, we collect a new dataset, WHOLE, using a UAV platform across Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. Extensive experiments on public benchmarks and WHOLE demonstrate competitive rendering quality and improved geometric accuracy relative to perspective systems. Compared with existing panoramic baselines, GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 5.56-9.10 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9-83.9%. To assess deployment feasibility on resource-constrained platforms such as UAVs, we evaluate an embedded configuration of GOLD-SLAM on a Jetson Orin NX (16 GB), demonstrating online operation at the cost of reconstruction quality.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Ground and aerial robots require reliable localization, dense geometry, and photorealistic rendering for interaction, often under limited sensor budget [20, 23]. LiDAR provides sparse geometric measurements with metric scale, IMUs supply high-frequency inertial constraints, and cameras capture dense color and texture. Their complementary roles underpin multisensor odometry and mapping systems [15, 21, 3335]. 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) [11] represents scenes using explicit anisotropic Gaussians. Its eﬀicient rasterization enables faster rendering than NeRF [19], promoting the development of Gaussian-based SLAM [9, 12, 13, 18, 22]. However, the narrow field of view (FoV) of perspective cameras limits scene coverage and inter-frame correspondences, making pose estimation more vulnerable to repetitive or sparse textures and rapid motion [7]. Panoramic cameras expand coverage to 360 180 spherical FoV, but their projections introduce stronger nonlinear distortion [8]. ODGS-SLAM [22] extends incremental Gaussian SLAM to equirectangular projection (ERP) images. However, it suffers from scale drift outdoors, motivating the use of LiDAR geometric constraints for large-scale mapping. 1 GOLD-SLAM Figure 1. The limited LiDAR coverage (colored points) in 360 panoramic images leads to large LiDAR blind-zone (percentages are solid-angle weighted) and multimodal fusion challenge. Panoramic LiDARinertialvisual Gaussian SLAM faces several technical challenges: 1. Nonuniform ERP sampling and polar distortion. ERP projection introduces nonuniform sampling on the sphere and substantial stretching near the poles [17, 22]. 2. Greater impact of the LiDAR blind zone. LiDARcamera FoV mismatch leaves regions without depth support [2, 13]. Panoramic coverage exposes more such regions, complicating Gaussian initialization  (Fig. 1)  . 3. Interference with new surface reconstruction. In incremental Gaussian SLAM, high accumulated opacity from existing Gaussians can block opacity-only insertion on newly observed nearby surfaces [10, 27]. Beyond these technical challenges, commonly used LiDARvisual benchmarks focus on ground-robot or handheld/backpack acquisition [24, 28, 30, 31], leaving UAV motion underrepresented. In this context, our contributions are: We present GOLD-SLAM, Gaussian splatting SLAM framework fusing LiDAR, IMU, and panoramic cameras with shared spherical model for tracking and mapping. We combine blind-zone visual constraints with Patch Brightness Uncertainty (PBU) to improve pose estimation under limited LiDAR coverage and illumination changes. We combine measured LiDAR depth with panoramic depth predictions for Gaussian initialization and design Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP) to improve incremental surface reconstruction. We collect WHOLE, dataset of LiDAR and IMU measurements and panoramic images acquired with customized UAV platform in indoor, outdoor, and degraded environments. Results on WHOLE and public benchmarks demonstrate competitive localization and improved geometric reconstruction with broad scene coverage.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Gaussian Splatting SLAM. 3DGS [11] enables eﬀicient photorealistic rendering through differentiable Gaussian rasterization. MonoGS [18] uses differentiable splatting for monocular SLAM, with analytic pose Jacobians and optional depth supervision. Photo-SLAM [9] combines geometric and photometric features with progressive Gaussian pyramid learning and geometric densification for monocular, stereo, and RGB-D SLAM. SplaTAM [10] and GS-SLAM [27] use depth-guided Gaussian insertion, with GS-SLAM also suppressing floating artifacts. Unlike these perspective systems, GOLD-SLAM performs panoramic reconstruction with LiDAR geometric supervision and predicted depth for blind-zone Gaussian initialization. Omnidirectional SLAM. Omnidirectional SLAM expands visual coverage through multi-camera systems or fisheye cameras. Gaussian projection and rendering must handle polar stretching and horizontal periodicity in ERP images. 360ORB-SLAM [3] combines panoramic features, triangulation, and depth completion for localization and point-cloud mapping. Panoramic LiDAR DSO [7] associates panoramic images with LiDAR 2 GOLD-SLAM Figure 2. Overview of GOLD-SLAM. The UAV platform collects LiDAR, IMU measurements and panoramic images. Inspired by FAST-LIVO2s error-state filtering framework [34], the frontend integrates panoramic visual updates with IMU propagation and LiDAR scan-to-map constraints. Inter-frame constraints use features in the LiDAR blind zone, while Patch Brightness Uncertainty (PBU) models shared brightness variations in the LiDAR-supported zone. To support panoramic reconstruction, we adapt the Gaussian-LIC2 backend [13] to spherical projection and rendering. Gaussians are initialized using measured LiDAR depth and predicted panoramic depth, and optimized with photometric and LiDAR depth losses. Depth-Aware Map Extension and Pruning (DAEP) combines depth-aware insertion, depth-guided adaptive updates, and depth-conflict pruning to improve the reconstruction of newly observed surfaces. observations for robust tracking. ODGS [14] reconstructs Gaussian scenes from ERP images, and ODGSSLAM [22] extends incremental Gaussian SLAM to ERP input. Multimodal Fusion. In large-scale scenes, multimodal fusion supports localization and reconstruction under visual degradation or LiDAR degeneracy. LIV-GaussMap [6] uses LiDARIMU poses and initial geometry, then refines Gaussians photometrically. Gaussian-LIC [12] combines tightly coupled LiDARIMUcamera localization with Gaussian initialization from LiDAR points and blind-zone visual triangulation. GS-LIVM [25] completes LiDAR surfaces via Gaussian process regression, using predicted covariance for Gaussian initialization. Gaussian-LIC2 [13] combines lightweight depth completion for blind-zone Gaussian initialization with LiDAR depth supervision. Building on this, GOLD-SLAM supports panoramic reconstruction and uses blind-zone visual constraints and PBU for pose estimation.

sections.title: 4.1 The WHOLE Dataset
sections.content: We build the WHOLE dataset with UAV motion under challenging geometric and illumination conditions, covering Weak-geometry, High-dynamic, Omnidirectional, Low-light, and Easy scenarios. It contains 20 sequences of panoramic images, LiDAR scans, and IMU measurements collected in indoor and outdoor campus environments. The scenes include rooms, long corridors, garages, glass facades, and open spaces  (Fig. 5)  . Recordings span daytime and nighttime conditions, low-light garages, and rapid motion with image blur. Some sequences combine these visual challenges with weak geometry, enabling evaluation of localization and reconstruction under simultaneous visual and geometric degradation. Data are collected using customized FanciSwarm Pro [1] UAV platform  (Fig. 2)  . The platform carries MID360S LiDAR with its built-in IMU and an Insta360 X5 dual-fisheye panoramic camera. We use Kalibr [5] with an AprilGrid to calibrate the intrinsics of both fisheye cameras and the cameraIMU spatial and temporal parameters. LiDARcamera extrinsics are calibrated with FAST-Calib2 [32]. AprilGrid observations provide reference poses at the sequence endpoints. Figure 5. Visualization of scenes from WHOLE: (a) indoor, (b,c) outdoor, (d,e) nighttime, and (f) garage.

sections.title: 4.2 Experimental Setup
sections.content: Datasets. In this work, we conduct experiments on five datasets. Table 1 summarizes the statistics and comparison between existing four datasets and WHOLE. From the Hilti-Oxford 2022 Dataset (Hilti-Oxford) [31], we select sequences covering construction site (Exp04), basement (Exp14), corridor and gallery (Exp18), and building exteriors (Exp21). M3DGR [30] provides sequences with varying illumination (Varying-illu05), long corridors (Corridor01/02), and outdoor grassy areas (Grass01/02). On M3DGR, GOLD-SLAM and GaussianLIC2 use MID-360 as their sole LiDAR input. M2DGR [28] covers indoor rooms and halls (room_01 and 6 GOLD-SLAM hall_02), an outdoor-to-indoor transition (door_02), and an outdoor gate area (gate_03). sections.title: 4.3 Localization Accuracy
sections.content: We first evaluate localization accuracy using ATE RMSE and translational endpoint drift. Across the public datasets, GOLD-SLAM achieves the lowest mean ATE on Hilti-Oxford and M3DGR, ranks second on Oxford Spires, and provides comparable accuracy on M2DGR  (Table 3)  . Long corridors challenge both LiDAR registration and visual tracking through repetitive geometry and appearance. In Table 4, FAST-LIO2 accumulates large drift on both corridors, while FAST-LIVO2 fails on Corridor01. On Corridor02, GOLD-SLAM reduces endpoint drift from 1.319 with FAST-LIVO2 to 0.274 m. sections.title: 4.4 Rendering and Geometric Reconstruction
sections.content: We evaluate in-sequence novel-view rendering and depth consistency on shared front views, with per-sequence results provided in Appendix J. In Table 5, GOLD-SLAM achieves the lowest mean Depth-L1 across all four public datasets and all four WHOLE groups, reducing the error by 2033% relative to Gaussian-LIC2 across WHOLE. GOLD-SLAM also leads most rendering comparisons, generally outperforming GaussianLIC2. GOLD-SLAM improves mean PSNR by 9.10 and 5.56 dB and reduces mean Depth-L1 by 71.9% and 83.9% relative to ODGS-SLAM and PanoGS-SLAM, respectively. This geometric advantage persists even though both panoramic baselines receive GOLD-SLAMs fused depth DF . Beyond depth completion, GOLDSLAM uses measured LiDAR depth to supervise map optimization. The DAP-only ablation in Table 7 supports the role of measured depth: replacing LiDAR measurements with predictions increases reconstruction error under the same frontend poses. 8 GOLD-SLAM Higher image fidelity need not imply more accurate surface geometry. For example, on Grass02, PanoGSSLAM achieves higher PSNR than GOLD-SLAM (22.87 vs. 18.92 dB), but also higher Depth-L1 (11.312 vs. 6.980 m; see Appendix J). Table 5. Results of in-sequence novel-view rendering and depth consistency on shared 512 384 front views (97 horizontal FoV). Values are means (sample standard deviations) over sequences; Depth-L1 is radial-depth MAE against LiDAR.

sections.title: 4.5 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Analysis of LiDAR Blind Zone. On Oxford Spires Keble03, we progressively crop the vertical LiDAR FoV used by the mapping backend while keeping its horizontal FoV and the frontend unchanged. The retained solidangle fraction decreases from 100% to 0% in 10-percentage-point steps. At = 0, Gaussian initialization relies entirely on DAP, without LiDAR scale alignment or depth supervision. As shown in Fig. 8, reducing from 100% to 50% decreases PSNR by only 0.33 dB, whereas Depth-L1 increases from 0.242 to 0.390 m. Further reductions in lead to more pronounced degradation in rendering quality and geometric accuracy. Without LiDAR support in the backend, Depth-L1 reaches 9.797 m. Figure 8. Analysis of LiDAR FoV on GOLD-SLAM. Each metric is independently minmax normalized. Analysis of Components. Table 7 evaluates system components on Hilti Exp18. Disabling blind-zone visual updates or PBU (σα = σb = 0) increases ATE from 0.100 to 0.161 or 0.158 m, respectively, and reduces PSNR from 25.42 dB to 23.08 dB or 24.92 dB. The three backend ablations share the frontend poses of the full model. No DAP initializes Gaussians only from LiDAR, reducing PSNR to 24.85 dB. DAP-only mapping uses only DAP for backend initialization and depth supervision, while its Depth-L1 rises from 0.450 to 1.223 m. No DAEP retains opacity-based insertion, reducing PSNR to 25.21 dB and increasing LPIPS from 0.189 to 0.214. This supports DAEPs role in reconstructing nearer surfaces that opacity-based insertion can miss when distant Gaussians provide high opacity  (Fig. 4)  . Full achieves the best PSNR, SSIM, LPIPS, and Depth-L1. Table 7. Ablation study of GOLD-SLAM components. Shading highlights key comparisons with the full model.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We present GOLD-SLAM, integrating omni-directional vision, LiDAR, and IMU with unified spherical tracking and Gaussian mapping. Blind-zone visual constraints and PBU support robust pose estimation. Measured LiDAR depth and panoramic depth predictions guide Gaussian initialization, while DAEP improves incremental surface reconstruction. Besides, we build WHOLE, novel multimodal dataset spanning handheld and UAV motion in challenging environments. Experiments show competitive localization and improved geometric accuracy and rendering quality with broad scene coverage. We hope this challenging task along with its dataset can bring new insight to the community. Limitation and Future Work. Our geometric evaluation is limited to regions with LiDAR reference depth. Future work will use simulated scenes with dense ground-truth geometry to assess blind-zone reconstruction. We will also improve panoramic stitching and temporal alignment to reduce the effects of multi-camera parallax and synchronization errors on tracking and mapping.

sections.title: A Embedded Deployment
sections.content: To assess computational feasibility for UAV applications, we evaluate an online implementation of GOLDSLAM on Jetson Orin NX with 16 GB of shared memory across all 37 benchmark sequences. Configuration. We use 512256 ERP/DAP inputs, FP16 DAP inference, degree-zero spherical harmonics, and 70 optimization views per update. Sensor data are replayed at 1 speed, with tracking and mapping running asynchronously. Evaluation and Results. Table 8 reports reconstruction quality, processing rates, and memory use. Four sequences fail due to out-of-memory (OOM) errors. The embedded configuration achieves mean PSNR of 19.51 dB, compared with 25.31 dB for the configuration used in the main experiments. Across the 17 completed WHOLE sequences, the mean endpoint drift is 0.333 m. Meanwhile, physical memory usage across the device peaks at 14.82 GiB. These results support the feasibility of embedded deployment for UAV applications, with reduced reconstruction quality and limited memory headroom under the tested configuration. Table 8. sections.title: F Panoramic Depth Estimator Ablation
sections.content: We compare DAP [3], BiFuse++ [6], and UniDAC [1] using public pretrained weights without fine-tuning. DAP achieves the lowest Render-Depth-L1 on four of the five sequences and the highest PSNR and SSIM on three  (Table 10)  . On gate_03, UniDAC has the lowest raw depth error, while DAP has the lowest rendered error after LiDAR alignment and depth supervision. Figure 9 shows that DAP generally produces clearer depth boundaries between foreground structures and the background. These reconstruction results favor DAP as the default estimator, while BiFuse++ has the shortest runtime and lowest peak VRAM usage on all five sequences. 16 GOLD-SLAM Supplementary Material Table 10. Panoramic depth estimator ablation. Raw-Depth-L1 measures prediction error before LiDAR scale alignment; Render-Depth-L1 measures final map error. Rendering metrics use in-sequence novel ERP views.

sections.title: G LiDAR Sampling Density Ablation
sections.content: Figure 10. LiDAR patch-size ablation. Each curve is minmax normalized. Vertical dashed lines mark the default 3 3 setting. To initialize Gaussians from LiDAR, we retain the valid point with the smallest radial depth in each ERP patch. We vary the patch size from 1 1 to 8 8 pixels on the first 600 input frames of Hilti-Oxford Exp21 and Oxford Spires Keble03, with DAP sampling fixed. Compared with 1 1 patches, 3 3 patches reduce the final Gaussian count by over 60% on both sequences, while lowering optimization time and peak VRAM usage. These savings come with PSNR drop below 0.3 dB and Depth-L1 increase below 0.02 m. Increasing the patch size beyond 3 3 saves more optimization time but lowers SSIM and raises LPIPS  (Fig. 10)  .

sections.title: H Keyframe Selection Ablation
sections.content: On the first 1,000 input frames of each sequence, we compare fixed-interval sampling (Fixed), co-visibility and depth-normalized translation (C+T) [4], spherical angular displacement (Parallax), and translation distance (Displacement). Fixed achieves the lowest LPIPS on four of the five sequences  (Table 11)  . On Observatory01, Parallax selects 351 keyframes versus 198 for Fixed, improving PSNR by 0.43 dB at more than twice the optimization time. We use Fixed as the default to keep the keyframe rate predictable while retaining competitive reconstruction quality. Table 11. Keyframe selection ablation on shared held-out ERP views.
